updates.note: Urged summer water conservation: follow the city watering schedule, water early or late, fix leaks; said updates go on the city website and social media and residents can sign up for city alerts.

First appearance. Lives in Calallen not far from the O.N. Stevens plant; keeps tomatoes on the watering schedule; wants the city to text residents when things change instead of learning from neighbors' posts days later.
Told Gulfwater the terminals are busy and tankers at the anchorage are "a sign of demand ... what a working export port looks like."
First appearance (Harborline 6). Opening his shop early for summer crowds; joke: customers want "shrimp, ice and directions," he only charges for two.

Announced depot hiring of helicopter mechanics, pitched to locals ("a lot of our mechanics grew up here ... and stayed"); depot trains new hires; openings on USAJOBS; welcomes people who've turned a wrench "in the military, at a refinery or on a shrimp boat."

Said summer is a normal training season and the base is operating normally; residents with noise or activity questions can contact public affairs: "We'd rather answer a question than have people guess."
Called Corpus Christi "where the Permian meets the water"; warned the hub's efficiency leaves "not much slack" and any pause in loadings hits freight schedules fast.

First appearance (profile). Age 67, lives on North Beach; spent 30+ years welding pipe and steel at refineries and fabrication yards along the ship channel; watches tankers from a lawn chair; "the bridge is your front door"; "every one of those ships is somebody's good work or somebody's shortcut."

At preparedness fair: "we need to know who you are and where you are before the storm, not during it"; registration through the state registry by dialing 2-1-1; registry covers anyone without transportation, not only people with disabilities.

First appearance. Attended a county preparedness fair with her youngest child (age 6); took an evacuation-assistance registration card home; rents a few blocks from the bay; "three kids and two bus routes." Left unresolved whether she submitted the card ("Ask me in a week").
First appearance. Age 59; brought a carload of church neighbors to the county fair; keeps her own notebook of neighbors without cars or phones; "A list in my notebook doesn't send a bus."
Told Anchor & Rotor veterans and military spouses bring the discipline depot work needs.
Told Anchor & Rotor military families get the same advice: know your zone, have a plan to leave, register now if no car.
Fact-check source: registry is for anyone without a way to leave, "Don't talk yourself out of it."
Health feature: checks the thermostat first at every client visit; some older female clients avoid AC because of the bill; carries two frozen water bottles on the bus; phones every client before bed.

First appearance. Owns a shrimp boat out of Aransas Pass; learned the bays on his father's boat; diesel is "the first bill and the biggest one"; pays fuel, ice and one deckhand per trip and still owes on the boat; "Three good days and one bad one, you're even."
Quoted on Pastor Gloria: "You don't call her. She calls you."

Profile. Spiral notebook (cracked cover, rubber band) of neighbors' needs in blue ink; list began years ago as a prayer list; Wednesday meals in the fellowship hall; she has a car ("God gave me a car and a loud voice"); goal: get everyone in her notebook onto the county registry.
Said the routine readiness inspection is complete; gates, clinic, commissary and flight line on normal hours; results not released.
Port proud of strategic-seaport role: "We'll work the military cargo alongside our regular business. Our people know how to do both."
Announced the Fort Hood aviation brigade's late-summer movement through the port for an overseas rotation; no date or destination; "We'll be ready to deploy when the port is ready for us."
To the Ledger: "Scheduling is what we do every day ... Everybody gets a slot, and everybody gets out on time."
Thanked personnel for inspection prep; nothing changes for families.
Re-quoted from the brigade announcement in Anchor & Rotor's weekly.
Re-quoted in Gulfwater on handling military cargo alongside regular business.
Explainer: "summer stretches every part of [the system] at once"; afternoon watering mostly evaporates; leaks and main breaks can be reported to the city.
Lives a few minutes from O.N. Stevens; neighbors will conserve but want plain-word updates from the city first, "not from a rumor at the gas station."
Announced Coastline Public Radio is mapping transportation access across the Coastal Bend this hurricane season and invited residents without cars to share evacuation plans.
Rents a duplex near the bay; weekday commute starts at a bus shelter at 6:10 a.m., transfer downtown, second bus, then a walk; "Everybody says, 'Just leave.' OK. In what?"
"A plan that starts with 'get in your car' isn't a plan for my street"; many people she feeds on Wednesdays have never owned a car; helping neighbors register.
"If you don't have a way out, tell us now. That's how we know where to send help."
To Harborline 6: "Registering is step one. Step two is somebody actually showing up"; wants more rides, pickup spots and door-knocking.

Wrote an opinion column calling for published neighborhood pickup points, partnerships with church hubs, and door-to-door outreach; says she watched Rosa Elizondo take a registration card at the fair.
Avoids crossing the Harbor Bridge on weekend afternoons; "out here the bridge isn't just a road. It's the door."
Coastline profile: keeps fuel receipts clipped to his truck visor; small crew; boat "old but sound"; calls the bay "a nursery"; "complaining about diesel. Not the bay. Never the bay."

Profile: after a county preparedness fair, built a contact list/phone tree for her Calallen street (who is older, lives alone, has a generator or truck, has young kids, lacks a smartphone); bought classroom supplies for fall; neighbors joke "Mrs. Ramos has a list."
Filed the wire story on a foreign government's announced naval and special-operations exercises (WASHINGTON dateline); no country named; analysts called it a show of force.
Welcomed new arrivals: "Everything's open ... come by and get your bearings."
Told new military arrivals to learn their zone "from us, not from the internet."
Explainer on show-of-force exercises; deliberately did not tie them to local units or the Fort Hood rotation.
Customers waiting in the lot before he unlocks ("Not all night").

Ledger profile: age 64; opens by 6 a.m.; live-bait tanks and a shell lot; shop a short walk from the jetties; rode out two hurricanes at the shop, one of them Harvey; tells tarpon lore (a president fished there; town once called Tarpon); "Everybody tells me I'm too old to do it again. Everybody's probably right." Did not say whether he'd ride out another.
Re-quoted in the Ledger's summer scorecard on fuel costs.
To the Ledger: "The export machine is running about as hard as it can ... very little slack."
Coastline feature: "These are careers, not gigs"; "Everything gets checked, and then it gets checked again"; hot hangars in August.
Fellowship hall shelves filling with canned goods, diapers and bottled water; "the first plate of food after a storm usually comes from somebody's church kitchen."

First appearance. Gulf Relief Logistics has standby relief contracts ("a reservation you hope you never use"); pre-plans lanes, boxes, drivers and alternate routes if a highway or the port closes; promises freight "in hours, not days"; "If it's not staged before the storm ... after is always slower."
"Buy a little every time you go to the store."
Helped sort donations at the church hub with her kids; "They help me all year. This is me helping back."
Fellowship hall now stocked like a warehouse with a whiteboard of needs; "Nobody brings batteries"; helping neighbors register via 2-1-1; "We already know who needs what. Use us."
Wrote an editor's-note opinion column; identifies herself as a longtime Navy spouse.

First appearance (pre-storm, Perseids). Age 42, Flour Bluff; films the night sky with a tripod camera on long runs; can tell meteors, satellites and air station training planes apart; "Once you know the regulars, anything new jumps out at you."
Warned of concentration risk: "When this much export capacity runs through one channel, you watch anything that could close that channel."

Ledger profile: Saturday pancakes; youngest (6) and oldest (a teenager); her evacuation plan is "a list of people who drive" (a neighbor, church friends, Pastor Gloria, the county); packed go-bag with documents, clothes, charger, kids' medicine and the fair flashlight. Still not stated whether she submitted the registry card.
